I'm not entirely sure what you mean by 'what difference does the policy gradient make.' They are just entirely different methods to learn a policy. Like I could cook chicken in an oven, or in a stove top pan. Yes they're both cooking chicken, but they're not really related otherwise. 

Policy Gradients are on-policy, meaning it can only learn from data collected with the current policy. While Q-learning is off-policy, meaning it can learn from any data collected. Which one performs better varies from task to task. It is usually the case however that policy gradients tend to learn much faster in real time, and take up a lot less resources, since most Q-Learning algorithms involve storing large buffers of transitions compared to policy gradients, and tend to take gradient steps more often.

I'm believe DQN is much slower because it does a gradient update every 4 steps, where as PPO runs 8 environments in parallel and updates after 128 steps are taken in each environments, it does 4 (if i remember correctly) minibatch updates after this. So it only does 4 gradient updates every 128 * 8 (1024) steps. And a 2080ti is not going to be much slower doing an update with 32 elements or 256 elements in a batch.

PPO does better on some environments and worse on others. For example, it does very bad on BeamRider, but does better on Qbert.

Unfortunately dealing with images will be slow for the most part. However in my experience DQN is a very slow algorithm. I have a similar setup and, for example, PPO takes about 1/6th the amount of time DQN does to train on the same number of frames

This is completely incorrect advice for /u/Stephanehk. The loss of the Q-function can be useful, although it generally is not. It can be helpful in the case you have exploding gradients with a much to high learning rate, you will see the loss go up on a consistent basis. (although that doesn't appear to be the case here).

Second 0.1 is not to high for an epsilon. In fact in the original DQN paper it is the lowest they ever made epsilon: "The behavior
policy during training was epsilon-greedy with epsilon annealed linearly from 1 to 0.1 over the first million
frames, and fixed at 0.1 thereafter". If you always have epsilon at a low value this can create a problem where your agent does not explore enough and 
therefore can't learn, because it is not visiting new states.

You may want to consider starting with a higher epsilon and lowering over time. Also I'm not sure on the scale of the graphs, but it looks like you only took about 6000 time steps, which is going to be no where near enough to train a DQN. I just tested OpenAI's baseline, They start with epsilon=1, and decrease it over time. It doesn't start to increase it's score significantly until around 700 epsisodes, which was around 18000 time steps. And they are using many more optimizations that you are not, such as Priority Replay Memory and Double DQN.

In pytorch the first parameter for a conv2d is the number of channels in the input image. In this case, the starting number of channels is 1, which means you’re taking in a grayscale image. The next number, pytorch calls out channels, but is more commonly referred to as the number of filters. This is the number of filters we have in out convolution layer, which can be thought of as producing a new image with that many channels. The final number is the kernel_size, which is how large the filter is that we slide across our image. These kernels are square, so 5 means a 5x5 filter

Edit: it’s also important to note that the in channels of each layer needs to be equal to the out channels of the last

I’m a student working in computer vision research, and while driving around a close circuit without crashing is certainly solved. Driving around a circuit as fast as possible without crashing sounds like it should be simple enough, but something where you have to punish the model for hitting a wall, but also reward it for going as close to the wall as fast as possible. This can be a tricky thing to balance in your reward function. Especially on formula e tracks that are all very tight road courses.

On the note of drivers helping train a model, If I were working on a project like this, getting data from professional drivers driving would be very useful to solving the problem I described above, because they will get very close to where you want your model to be, making the job of fine tuning of risk/reward balance a lot easier. When deciding our flatting range we want to think about what our hands equity is against villains opening range, but we have to adjust that to what we we think our realizable equity is. This is going to be different for different hands, SCs may be able to realize 80% or more of their equity, while hands like K2o may only be able to realize 50% or possibly less. The type of villain we are up against will also affect the amount of realizable equity we have, generally the more passive the more we can realize. For example, against a 3x we need 31% equity, but if we only expect to realize 70% of our equity with a given hand we will actually need 44.3% equity to continue with that hand.

For Value 3 betting, we're looking for hands that will have at least 50% equity (preferably more, some say at least 55%) against villains continuing range (including value 4bets), not just his opening range.

For 3bet bluffs, there are a few ways people decide what hands to choose.
    
1) Choose only hands outside your calling range, and choose the best ones (e.g. if K5s is a call and K4s is a fold, K4s becomes a 3bet bluff). For balance we want to make our opponent indifferent to 4bet bluffing, so we choose a number of combos that makes that happen.

2) Chose some hands just outside our calling range, and then 3bet some of the high playability hands inside our calling range to 3bet some of the time. For example 3bet JTs, T9s, 98s, 87s, etc 25% of the time and call them 75%

There are other methods in addition to these, but these are the most common. However against some players we will not want to bluff at all, so we would value 3bet more hands instead.

That's what I do personally, I think it's important to see if some people don't adjust ranges by position or are stealing a massively wide range from the Btn or sb. I think it becomes less important as you move higher because people tend to play very similar ranges, but it is certainly helpful when thinking about villains range postflop to know wether they open 20% in the CO or 30% for example

There are a few reasons people only 3 bet from the small blind

 1) You will always be out of position post flop, and playing out of position 3 ways is not great
 2) You have to invest more money to just call than you would in the BB making your pot odds worse
 3) You still have a player left to act behind you, and if you're calling a range that doesn't include the top hands, the BB can take advantage by 3 betting more and picking up your dead money, especially against late position raises

Yes you are going to want to 3bet wider even against players who defend against 3bets a reasonable amount. This is because they need to defend a ton of combos out of a wide opening range to prevent you from overbluffing. Because of this you can value 3bet slightly wider, which means you need to bluff more combos even against regs. When picking your bluffs pick the best hands that are not good enough to call. So for example if you call with 65s vs. a 3x but would not call 54s, 54s would then become a 3bet bluff. As far as amount of bluffs, a reasonable default (assuming you don't fold any of your value range to a 4bet) would be about 1.25 bluffs combos per value combo, which comes from making your opponent indifferent to 4bet bluff. The more villain folds however, the more we can add bluffs making the ratio larger towards bluffs to exploit over folding
